claim: In uncertain or unstable environments, the best decision is sometimes to change your mind.
source: In uncertain or unstable environments, sometimes the best decision is to change your mind.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract introducing the research topic.

claim: Continuous estimates of conflict and volatility contributed to shifts in exploratory states by changing both the rate of evidence accumulation (drift rate) and the amount of evidence needed to make a decision (boundary height).
source: Continuous estimates of conflict and volatility contributed to shifts in exploratory states by changing both the rate of evidence accumulation (drift rate) and the amount of evidence needed to make a decision (boundary height), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following a switch in the optimal choice, the drift rate plummets and the boundary height weakly spikes, leading to a slow exploratory state.
source: At the trialwise level, following a switch in the optimal choice, the drift rate plummets and the boundary height weakly spikes, leading to a slow exploratory state.
evidence: This is based on the trial-by-trial analysis of decision parameters around change points.

claim: The drift rate drives most of the response to a change point, with an unreliable contribution of boundary height across experiments.
source: We find that the drift rate drives most of this response, with an unreliable contribution of boundary height across experiments.
evidence: This is based on comparing results from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: There is no evidence that pupillary responses associated with decision policy changes.
source: Surprisingly, we find no evidence that pupillary responses associated with decision policy changes.
evidence: This is based on the pupillometry analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Humans show a stereotypical shift in their decision policies in response to environmental changes.
source: We conclude that humans show a stereotypical shift in their decision policies in response to environmental changes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The shift of a decision policy from exploratory to exploitative states is driven by environmental context.
source: The shift of a decision policy from exploratory to exploitative states is driven by environmental context.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations and experimental manipulations.

claim: Increasing either conflict or volatility led to selecting agents with more random or exploratory selection policies in Q-learning simulations.
source: Increasing either form of uncertainty led to selecting agents with more random or exploratory selection policies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on Q-learning agent simulations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: As the value of the optimal choice decreases relative to the value of a suboptimal choice (conflict increases), the learner exploits what she already knows.
source: As the value of the optimal choice decreases relative to the value of a suboptimal choice (conflict increases), the learner exploits what she already knows.
evidence: This is inferred from the Q-learning simulation results.

claim: When action values grow unstable (volatility increases) and the clarity of the optimal choice is constant (constant conflict), the learner is biased toward exploration.
source: Action values grow unstable (volatility increases) when the clarity of the optimal choice is constant (constant conflict), and the learner is biased toward exploration (Bland and Schaefer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and cited literature.

claim: The drift diffusion model proposes that a decision between two choices is described by a noisy accumulation process that drifts toward one of two decision boundaries at a specific rate.
source: The normative form of the DDM proposes that a decision between two choices is described by a noisy accumulation process that drifts toward one of two decision boundaries at a specific rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the established DDM framework.

claim: Decreasing the drift rate and increasing the boundary height leads to more random decisions.
source: For example, decreasing the drift rate and increasing the boundary height leads to more random decisions (Figure 1C), with the speed of these decisions depending on the ratio of the two parameters (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through DDM simulations shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Exploratory policies can result in either fast or slow decisions, depending on the relative configuration of drift rate and boundary height.
source: Thus, exploratory policies can result in either fast or slow decisions, depending on the relative configuration of drift rate and boundary height.
evidence: This is inferred from the DDM simulation results.

claim: The parameters of a DDM process can be modulated by feedback signals and choice history.
source: Previous modeling work has shown that the parameters of a DDM process can be modulated by feedback signals and choice history (Pedersen et al., 2017; Ratcliff and Frank, 2012; Dunovan and Verstynen, 2019; Dunovan et al., 2019; Mendonça et al., 2020; Urai et al., 2018) with different mechanisms for adapting the drift rate and the boundary height.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: In value-based decision-making tasks where the statistics of sensory signals are equivalent for all actions, drift rate fluctuations appear to track the relative value of an action or the value difference between actions.
source: In value-based decision-making tasks where the statistics of sensory signals are equivalent for all actions, drift rate fluctuations appear to track the relative value of an action or the value difference between actions (Dunovan et al., 2019; Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016; Bariselli et al., 2019; Rubin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Selection errors in value-based decision-making have been linked to changes in the boundary height.
source: In contrast to value estimation, selection errors in this context have been linked to changes in the boundary height (Forstmann et al., 2008; Forstmann et al., 2010; Bogacz et al., 2010; Herz et al., 2016; Herz et al., 2017; Dunovan et al., 2019; Dunovan and Verstynen, 2019) and internal estimates of environmental change (Nassar et al., 2010; Wilson and Niv, 2011; Nassar et al., 2012; Behrens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The locus coeruleus norepinephrine (LC-NE) system has been linked to adaptive behavioral variability in response to uncertainty.
source: One plausible neural mechanism for this migration along the surface of selection policies is the locus coereleus norepinephrine (LC-NE) system, which has been linked to adaptive behavioral variability in response to uncertainty (Urai et al., 2017; Dayan and Yu, 2006; Bouret and Sara, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The LC-NE system has two distinct modes (phasic and tonic) that map onto distinct decision states.
source: The LC-NE system has two distinct modes (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981) that map onto distinct decision states (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: In the phasic mode, a burst of LC activity results in a global, temporally precise release of NE, which increases the gain on cortical processing and encourages exploitation.
source: In the phasic mode, a burst of LC activity results in a global, temporally precise release of NE. This increases the gain on cortical processing and encourages exploitation.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about LC-NE function.

claim: In the tonic mode, NE is released without the temporal precision of the phasic mode, increasing baseline NE and encouraging disengagement from the current task and facilitating exploration.
source: In the tonic mode, NE is released without the temporal precision of the phasic mode, increasing baseline NE (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981). This encourages disengagement from the current task and facilitates exploration.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about LC-NE function.

claim: The LC-NE system can be indirectly measured by fluctuations in pupil diameter.
source: Thus the LC-NE system, which can be indirectly measured by fluctuations in pupil diameter (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Jepma and Nieuwenhuis, 2011), may be a central mechanism for modulating selection policies.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: In Experiment 1, 24 participants completed four sessions (high and low conflict; high and low volatility) each composed of 600 trials.
source: In Experiment 1, 24 participants completed four sessions (high and low conflict; high and low volatility) each composed of 600 trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, four participants completed nine sessions composed of 400 trials each, generating 3600 trials in total per subject.
source: Four participants completed nine sessions composed of 400 trials each, generating 3600 trials in total per subject.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Experiment 2 manipulated the same forms of uncertainty as Experiment 1, but had different perceptual features and more expansively sampled the space of conflict and volatility.
source: Importantly, Experiment 2 manipulated the same forms of uncertainty as Experiment 1, but had different perceptual features and more expansively sampled the space of conflict and volatility.
evidence: This describes the relationship between the two experiments.

claim: In Experiment 1, only the boundary height and drift rate showed change point sensitivity.
source: Under this analysis, we found that only the boundary height and drift rate showed change point sensitivity as defined above.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical drift diffusion modeling of Experiment 1 data.

claim: There is strong evidentiary support for a mapping between value-driven belief and drift rate.
source: Altogether, this suggests that we have strong evidentiary support for a mapping between value-driven belief and drift rate (Figure 6A, blue).
evidence: This is based on model comparison results from both experiments.

claim: The support for a mapping between change point probability and boundary height, while robustly present in Experiment 1, fails to appear when tested in an independent data set (Experiment 2).
source: However, the support for a mapping between change point probability and boundary height (Figure 6A, red), while robustly present in Experiment 1, fails to appear when tested in an independent data set.
evidence: This is based on comparing model results between Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Following a shift in response contingencies, the navigation of the decision surface follows a stereotyped pattern in Experiment 1.
source: For Experiment 1, following a shift in response contingencies, the navigation of this decision surface follows a stereotyped pattern. The boundary height spikes and drift rate decreases rapidly, gradually recovering and stabilizing over time (see the trial prior to the change point in Figure 7A). This decision trajectory is robust in Experiment 1 (Figure 7B, top panel).
evidence: This is based on decision vector analysis of Experiment 1 data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the decision trajectory is substantially more variable than in Experiment 1, with most of the response restricted to the drift rate dimension and inconsistent trajectories along the boundary height dimension.
source: However, this trajectory is substantially more variable in Experiment 2, with most of the response restricted to the drift rate dimension and inconsistent trajectories along the boundary height dimension (Figure 7B, lower panel).
evidence: This is based on decision vector analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: In both experiments, the decision trajectory quickly responds to a shift in action outcomes and also quickly recovers and stabilizes.
source: In both experiments, we find that the decision trajectory quickly responds to a shift in action outcomes and also quickly recovers and stabilizes.
evidence: This is based on decision vector analysis of both experiments.

claim: In Experiment 2, the evoked response model describing the relationship between shifts in decision parameters and time relative to a change point was more probable than the null model.
source: We found that the evoked response model describing the relationship between shifts in decision parameters and time relative to a change point was more probable than the null model (see Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian circular regression model comparison.

claim: In Experiment 2, the relationship between the rate of evidence accumulation and the boundary height is only related to the change point itself, with no evidence that changing the degree of volatility or conflict changes the path of the decision policy following a change point.
source: These analyses suggest that the relationship between the rate of evidence accumulation and the boundary height is only related to the change point itself. We find no evidence to suggest that changing the degree of volatility or changing the degree of conflict changes the path of the decision policy following a change point.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian circular regression model comparison.

claim: The stereotyped response of the decision policy is solely dependent on the presence of a change point rather than either the history of change point frequency or the history of optimal choice ambiguity.
source: Thus, the stereotyped response of the decision policy is solely dependent on the presence of a change point rather than either the history of change point frequency or the history of optimal choice ambiguity.
evidence: This is inferred from the model comparison results.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was no evidence that the pupillary response associates with the dynamics of the decision policy changes in response to a change in action-outcome contingencies.
source: We find no evidence that the pupillary response associates with the dynamics of the decision policy changes in response to a change in action-outcome contingencies.
evidence: This is based on pupillometry analysis and model comparison.

claim: The first two principal components of pupillary metrics explained 95% of the variance in the pupillary data.
source: We found that the first two principal components explained 95% of the variance in the pupillary data.
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: Peak onset, peak offset, and latency to peak amplitude had the greatest feature importance for the first principal component of pupillary metrics.
source: Peak onset, peak offset, and latency to peak amplitude had the greatest feature importance for the first principal component (Figure 9B, upper panel).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: Mean pupil diameter and peak amplitude had the greatest feature importance for the second principal component of pupillary metrics.
source: Mean pupil diameter and peak amplitude had the greatest feature importance for the second principal component (Figure 9B, lower panel).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: In the context of volatile two-choice decisions, humans adopt a mechanism that simultaneously changes the rate of evidence accumulation and, sometimes, the threshold of evidence needed to trigger a decision, so as to adapt to an environmental change.
source: Our results suggest that, in the context of volatile two-choice decisions, humans adopt a mechanism that simultaneously changes the rate of evidence accumulation and, sometimes, the threshold of evidence needed to trigger a decision, so as to adapt to an environmental change (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: As soon as a shift in action outcomes is suspected, an internal estimate of change point probability increases and an estimate of the belief in the value of the optimal target plummets.
source: As soon as a shift in action outcomes is suspected, an internal estimate of change point probability increases and an estimate of the belief in the value of the optimal target plummets (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on the ideal observer analysis.

claim: The rapid increase in change point probability causes a rapid rise in the boundary height on the subsequent trial, thereby increasing the criterion for selecting a new action and allowing variability in the accumulation process to have a greater influence on choice, although this latter effect is inconsistent across experiments.
source: The rapid increase in change point probability causes a rapid rise in the boundary height on the subsequent trial, thereby increasing the criterion for selecting a new action and allowing variability in the accumulation process to have a greater influence on choice (Figure 7B), although this latter effect is inconsistent across experiments.
evidence: This is based on the HDDM regression results.

claim: When a learner confronts a change point, the decision policy becomes more exploratory by simultaneously increasing the amount of evidence needed to make a decision and slowing the integration of evidence over time.
source: These results show that when a learner confronts a change point, the decision policy becomes more exploratory by simultaneously increasing the amount of evidence needed to make a decision and slowing the integration of evidence over time.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Random exploration is driven by changes in the drift rate and the boundary height, with drift rate changes dominating the policy shift.
source: Feng and colleagues recently found that random exploration is driven by changes in the drift rate and the boundary height, with drift rate changes dominating the policy shift (Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: When environmental conditions encouraged exploration, the drift rate slowed, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio of the reward representation.
source: When environmental conditions encouraged exploration, the drift rate slowed, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio of the reward representation.
evidence: This is based on cited literature (Feng et al., 2020).

claim: During a modified reactive inhibitory control task, different feedback signals target different parts of the accumulation-to-bound process, with errors in response timing driving rapid changes in the drift rate on subsequent trials, while selection errors changed the boundary height.
source: Previous work by our lab (Dunovan and Verstynen, 2019) has shown how, during a modified reactive inhibitory control task, different feedback signals target different parts of the accumulation-to-bound process. Specifically, errors in response timing drove rapid changes in the drift rate on subsequent trials, while selection errors (i.e. making a response on trials where the response should be inhibited) changed the boundary height.
evidence: This is based on cited work from the authors' lab.

claim: The drift rate adapts on the basis of previous choices, independent of the feedback given for those choices.
source: Further, there is new evidence that the drift rate adapts on the basis of previous choices, independent of the feedback given for those choices.
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Choice history signals sculpt the dynamics of the accumulation process by biasing the rate of evidence accumulation.
source: Urai and colleagues have convincingly demonstrated that choice history signals sculpt the dynamics of the accumulation process by biasing the rate of evidence accumulation (Urai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: The experimental design cannot distinguish between pupillary dynamics driven by other catecholamines, such as dopamine, and those dynamics driven by the LC-NE system.
source: It should be noted, however, that our experimental design cannot distinguish between pupillary dynamics driven by other catecholamines, such as dopamine, and those dynamics driven by the LC-NE system (Spiers and Calne, 1969; McClure et al., 2005; Gershman and Tzovaras, 2018; Gershman and Uchida, 2019),
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: It is possible that the LC-NE system may still be playing a role in shift of decision policies, and the pupil responses collected were insensitive to the underlying dynamics.
source: Thus it is possible that the LC-NE system may still be playing a role in shift of decision policies, and the pupil responses we collected were insensitive to the underlying dynamics.
evidence: This is speculation about the null pupillometry findings.

claim: The cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) pathways are a crucial pathway for accumulating evidence during decision making.
source: Both recent experimental (Yartsev et al., 2018; Dunovan et al., 2015) and theoretical (Bogacz and Larsen, 2011; Caballero et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2015) studies have pointed to the CBGT loops as being a crucial pathway for accumulating evidence during decision making, with the wiring architecture of these pathways ideal for implementing the sequential probability ratio test (Bogacz and Gurney, 2007; Bogacz, 2007), the statistically optimal algorithm for evidence accumulation decisions and the basis for the DDM itself (Ratcliff, 1978).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Within the CBGT pathways, the difference in direct pathway activity between action channels covaries with the rate of evidence accumulation for individual decisions.
source: Further, multiple lines of theoretical work have suggested that, within the CBGT pathways, the difference in direct pathway activity between action channels covaries with the rate of evidence accumulation for individual decisions (Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016; Bariselli et al., 2019; Dunovan et al., 2019; Rubin et al., 2021),
evidence: This is based on cited theoretical work.

claim: The indirect pathways in the CBGT are linked to control of the boundary height.
source: while the indirect pathways are linked to control of the boundary height (Wei et al., 2015; Herz et al., 2016; Bogacz, 2007; Ratcliff and Frank, 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited theoretical work.

claim: Changes in the direct and indirect pathways, both within and between representations of different actions, may regulate shifts in decision policies.
source: This suggests that changes in the direct and indirect pathways, both within and between representations of different actions, may regulate shifts in decision policies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited literature and current findings.

claim: The CBGT pathways are a target of the dopaminergic signaling that drives reinforcement learning.
source: Critically, the CBGT pathways are a target of the dopaminergic signaling that drives reinforcement learning (Schultz et al., 1992), suggesting that changes in relative action-value should drive trial-by-trial changes in the drift rate.
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Dopamine may play a critical role in modulating decision policies.
source: Indeed, previous work relating dopaminergic circuitry to decision policy adaptation suggests that dopamine may play a critical role in modulating decision policies.
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Dopamine has substantial links to exploration.
source: Dopamine has substantial links to exploration (Kakade and Dayan, 2002) and recent pharmacological evidence suggests a role for dopaminergic regulation of exploration in humans (Chakroun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Both directed and random exploration have been linked to variations in genes that affect dopamine levels in prefrontal cortex and striatum, respectively.
source: More explicitly, both directed and random exploration have been linked to variations in genes that affect dopamine levels in prefrontal cortex and striatum, respectively (Gershman and Tzovaras, 2018).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: A dopamine-controlled spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule alters the ratio of direct to indirect pathway efficacy in a simulated corticostriatal network.
source: Physiologically, previous work has found that a dopamine-controlled spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule alters the ratio of direct to indirect pathway efficacy in a simulated corticostriatal network (Vich et al., 2020),
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Overall indirect pathway activity (i.e. pre-decision firing rates) is linked to the modulation of the boundary height in a DDM.
source: with overall indirect pathway activity (i.e. pre-decision firing rates) linked to the modulation of the boundary height in a DDM and the difference in direct pathway activation across action channels associating with changes in the drift rate (Dunovan et al., 2019; Rubin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Activating the subthalamic nucleus not only halts the motoric response but also interrupts cognitive processes related to action selection.
source: Moreover, recent optogenetic work in mice suggests that activating the subthalamic nucleus, a key node in the indirect pathway, not only halts the motoric response but also interrupts cognitive processes related to action selection (Heston et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: The decision policy reconfiguration observed may associate with belief-driven changes to drift rate varying with the difference in direct pathway firing rates across action channels, and change-point-probability-driven changes to the boundary height varying with overall indirect pathway activity.
source: Our current observations, combined with this previous work, suggests that the decision policy reconfiguration that we observe may associate with similar underlying corticostriatal dynamics, with belief-driven changes to drift rate varying with the difference in direct pathway firing rates across action channels (Dunovan et al., 2019), and change-point-probability-driven changes to the boundary height varying with overall indirect pathway activity (Dunovan et al., 2019; Vich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Carnegie Mellon University Institutional Review Board (Approval Code: 2018_00000195).
source: All procedures were approved by the Carnegie Mellon University Institutional Review Board (Approval Code: 2018_00000195; Funding: Air Force Research Laboratory, Grant Office ID: 180119).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All research participants provided informed consent to participate in the study and consent to publish any research findings based on their provided data.
source: All research participants provided informed consent to participate in the study and consent to publish any research findings based on their provided data.
evidence: This is a statement about informed consent.

claim: Twenty-four participants (19 female, 22 right-handed, 19–31 years old) were recruited for Experiment 1 and paid $20 at the end of four sessions.
source: Twenty-four participants (19 female, 22 right-handed, 19–31 years old) were recruited for Experiment 1 and paid $20 at the end of four sessions.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 1.

claim: Four participants (two female, 4 right-handed, 21–28 years old) were recruited for Experiment 2 and paid $10 for each of nine sessions, in addition to a performance bonus.
source: Four participants (two female, 4 right-handed, 21–28 years old) were recruited for Experiment 2 and paid $10 for each of nine sessions, in addition to a performance bonus.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 2.

claim: Hypotheses were registered prior to the completion of data collection using the Open Science Framework.
source: Hypotheses were registered prior to the completion of data collection using the Open Science Framework (Foster, MSLS and Deardorff, MLIS, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about preregistration.
